approachQuestion.prompt:
Roadside water

A vehicle starts at coordinate 0 with a full tank that supports R distance. Its destination is D>0. An increasing array s lists water stations strictly between 0 and D; each refill restores the full range R. Return the minimum number of refills, or -1 if the route is impossible. Starting full and arriving at D do not count as refills.

Example 1: s=[3,5,8], R=5, D=11 → 2; refill at 5 and 8.
Example 2: s=[2,8], R=5, D=10 → -1.
Example 3: s=[], R=8, D=8 → 0.

Constraints: 0 ≤ n ≤ 200000; 1 ≤ R,D ≤ 10^9; 0 < s[i] < D; station coordinates are distinct and already sorted. Input is read-only. Return only the stated scalar result. All arithmetic and comparisons use constant-time exact 64-bit operations; all intermediate values fit.

options.text: From the current refill position, scan forward to the farthest station reachable within R. If D is reachable, finish. Otherwise refill at that farthest station, or return -1 if no forward station is reachable. Never move the station index backward.
options.feedback: Any feasible next refill is no farther than the farthest reachable station. Refilling farther ahead leaves a destination frontier at least as far forward after the same number of refills, so replacing an earlier stop cannot increase the required count.

options.text: Refill at every station encountered before the destination.
options.feedback: This wastes stops and may still need an impossibility check. For s=[1,2,3], R=5, D=5, zero refills suffice rather than three.

options.text: Count the ceiling of D/R minus one, ignoring station positions.
options.feedback: The necessary refill locations may be absent. For s=[], R=3, D=5, the formula gives one but the route is impossible.

options.text: Enumerate every legal sequence of decisions, evaluate each complete candidate, and return the best result.
options.feedback: Exhaustive search can find the right result, but revisits combinations of decisions that the safe local rule resolves directly. The number of candidates grows far beyond what the input limit permits.

complexityQuestion.prompt: Analyze only the revealed frontier method, regardless of your previous choice. Use exactly the frontier method above as iterative scans with scalar indices, counters and accumulators. Do not copy the input and do not store a decision list. Let n be the number of input records or positions. Choose the tightest standard worst-case time and auxiliary-space pair.
constraints: Input and returned scalar are excluded. All other live storage, including copying and any call stack, is counted. No hashing or expected-time operations are used.

feedback.reason: The station index only advances; each stop is summarized by scalar reach state.

messages.text: The method stores no per-item history or copied input.
The scans do not restart for each item.
In the worst case every input item can affect the answer.

details: The station index never moves backward, so scanning across several refills still visits at most n stations in total. Current position, farthest feasible station, stop count, and index are scalars, giving O(1) auxiliary space.
“Time O(n), auxiliary space O(n)”: The method stores no per-item history or copied input.
“Time O(n²), auxiliary space O(1)”: The scans do not restart for each item.
“Time O(1), auxiliary space O(1)”: In the worst case every input item can affect the answer.
